Dimensionality reduction

Source: vignettes/articles/dimensionality-reduction.Rmd
dimensionality-reduction.Rmd

fs_pca() and fs_svd() reduce dimension without selecting features. They replace the original columns with a few new ones, each a weighted sum of all the inputs. You still have to measure every variable, and the new columns are chosen without reference to any outcome: they point in the directions of largest variance, which need not be the directions that predict anything. If you need to name the features you keep, use one of the filters, regularization methods, or wrappers instead.

Use fs_pca() on a data frame when you want tidy, labeled output: variance explained, loadings, scores next to your label columns, and a plot. Use fs_svd() on a numeric matrix when you want the raw singular values and vectors, for compression or as input to your own code.

Both functions return a plain list, not an fs_result, so selected() and the other fs_result helpers do not apply.

fs_pca()

Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the orthogonal directions along which the data vary most. The first component is the direction of largest variance, the second is the largest among directions perpendicular to the first, and so on.

fs_pca() runs a PCA on the numeric columns of a data frame. Character, factor, logical, and date columns are kept aside as labels, as is the column named in label_col. By default it keeps two components; set num_pc for more.

pca <- fs_pca(iris, num_pc = 2, label_col = "Species")
names(pca)
#> [1] "pc_loadings"   "pc_scores"     "var_explained" "pca_df"       
#> [5] "meta"          "plot"
pca$var_explained
#> [1] 0.7296245 0.2285076
pca$pc_loadings
#>                     PC1         PC2
#> Sepal.Length  0.5210659 -0.37741762
#> Sepal.Width  -0.2693474 -0.92329566
#> Petal.Length  0.5804131 -0.02449161
#> Petal.Width   0.5648565 -0.06694199
head(pca$pca_df)
#>          PC1        PC2 Species
#>        <num>      <num>  <fctr>
#> 1: -2.257141 -0.4784238  setosa
#> 2: -2.074013  0.6718827  setosa
#> 3: -2.356335  0.3407664  setosa
#> 4: -2.291707  0.5953999  setosa
#> 5: -2.381863 -0.6446757  setosa
#> 6: -2.068701 -1.4842053  setosa

How to read the output:

  • var_explained is the share of the total variance each retained component carries. On iris the first two components carry 73.0% and 22.9%, so together they keep about 96% of the variance in the four measurements. The vector sums to 1 only when you keep every component.
  • pc_loadings holds the weights (prcomp()’s rotation), one row per input column. PC1 weights the petal measurements and sepal length about equally (0.52 to 0.58), while PC2 is mostly sepal width (-0.92). The sign of a component is arbitrary: a component and its negation describe the same direction, so compare loadings within a column, not their signs across runs.
  • pc_scores holds each observation’s coordinates on the components, and pca_df is the same scores with the label columns bound alongside.

By default columns are centered and scaled (scale_data = TRUE), so the PCA runs on the correlation matrix. Leave scaling on unless every column is in the same meaningful units; otherwise the column with the largest variance dominates the first component. Scaling without centering (scale_data = TRUE, center_data = FALSE) is an error.

Missing values and constant columns

Before the decomposition, fs_pca() drops every row with a missing value in the numeric columns, and it drops every column with zero variance with a warning. Infinite values are an error. meta records what was used:

pca$meta$n_rows_used
#> [1] 150
pca$meta$numeric_cols
#> [1] "Sepal.Length" "Sepal.Width"  "Petal.Length" "Petal.Width"

iris has no missing values, so all 150 rows are used. On real data, check meta$n_rows_used and meta$rows_kept: a few gappy columns can remove most of the rows without an error. num_pc cannot exceed the number of usable columns, or the number of usable rows minus one.

Plotting

fs_pca() builds a ggplot of PC1 against PC2, colored by label_col, whenever a label_col is supplied, at least two components are kept, and ggplot2 is installed. The plot is returned in $plot; plot = TRUE also prints it.

pca$plot

When no plot can be built, the list has no plot element at all, so test with "plot" %in% names(pca).

Large data

Below 10 million cells (rows times numeric columns), fs_pca() uses stats::prcomp(). At or above that size it uses bigstatsr::big_SVD() on a temporary file-backed matrix, if bigstatsr is installed, and computes only the requested components; without bigstatsr it falls back to prcomp(). This engine can return at most one fewer component than there are columns, so num_pc equal to the number of columns is an error on large data. The large-data engine recovers the total variance from column statistics, so var_explained is still the share of the whole and not of the components that were computed.

Leakage

PCA never looks at the outcome, but it does learn from the rows it sees: the centering, scaling, and loadings all come from the data. If you fit it on all rows and then cross-validate a model on the scores, the test rows have shaped the features. fs_pca() does not return the centering and scaling values or a way to project new rows. To apply a PCA learned on training rows to test rows, fit stats::prcomp() on the training rows and call predict() on it. See Validation and leakage for the general rule.

fs_svd()

The singular value decomposition (SVD) factors a matrix X into U D V': D holds the singular values in decreasing order, and the columns of U and V are the left and right singular vectors. Keeping the first k triplets gives the best rank-k approximation of X.

fs_svd() is the lower-level tool. It takes a numeric matrix x (or an all-numeric data frame) and returns the singular values and vectors:

m <- as.matrix(mtcars)
s <- fs_svd(m, n_singular_values = 3, scale_input = TRUE)
round(s$singular_values, 3)
#> [1] 14.313  9.064  4.409
dim(s$left_singular_vectors)
#> [1] 32  3
dim(s$right_singular_vectors)
#> [1] 11  3

The left singular vectors have one row per observation (32 cars) and the right singular vectors one row per column (11 variables), each with one column per kept triplet. By default, n_singular_values = NULL keeps all of them, min(dim(x)).

x must not contain NA, NaN, or Inf. Unlike fs_pca(), fs_svd() drops nothing for you, so remove or impute missing values first.

scale_input = TRUE (the default) centers and scales the columns first, so the triplets factor scale(x), not x. The column means and standard deviations are not returned; keep them yourself if you need to map results back to the original units. The other options are FALSE (use x as is), "center", and "scale", which follows base::scale() and, without centering, divides by the root mean square rather than the standard deviation. The dividing forms stop with an error if a column has zero variance.

On centered and scaled data, the squared singular values divided by n - 1 are the PCA eigenvalues, so fs_svd() and prcomp() agree:

all_sv <- fs_svd(m)$singular_values
round(all_sv^2 / (nrow(m) - 1), 4)[1:3]
#> [1] 6.6084 2.6505 0.6272
round(prcomp(m, scale. = TRUE)$sdev^2, 4)[1:3]
#> [1] 6.6084 2.6505 0.6272

Exact or approximate

svd_method = "auto" uses base::svd() unless both of these hold: you ask for fewer singular values than min(dim(x)), and the smaller dimension of the matrix is larger than svd_threshold (default 100). Then it uses RSpectra::svds(), which computes only the leading triplets and needs the RSpectra package. svd_method = "approx" forces the approximate solver; if you ask for all min(dim(x)) values it falls back to the exact solver with a message, because RSpectra::svds() cannot return the full set. If RSpectra converges on fewer values than requested, featR warns and recomputes them exactly.

On a 400 by 150 matrix, the five leading singular values from both solvers agree to within 1e-6:

set.seed(1)
big <- matrix(rnorm(400 * 150), 400, 150)
approx <- fs_svd(big, n_singular_values = 5, svd_method = "approx")
exact  <- fs_svd(big, n_singular_values = 5, svd_method = "exact")
all.equal(approx$singular_values, exact$singular_values, tolerance = 1e-6)
#> [1] TRUE

Singular vectors are unique only up to sign, so the two solvers, or two platforms, can return columns with opposite signs. Compare vectors with abs() or through the reconstructed matrix, not element by element.
